title: Nanostructured bainite transformation characteristics in medium-carbon steel subjected to ausforming and isothermal holding below martensite start temperature
abstract: The influence of martensite on the transformation rate of bainite as well as enhancement of various properties is well established, yet the combined influence of both the primary martensite and low temperature ausforming below the martensite start temperature (MS) on the characteristics of microstructural evolution comprising ultrafine/nanostructured bainite, martensite and retained austenite (RA) in medium C steels has not been unambiguously clarified. A series of physical simulation experiments involving isothermal holding at various temperatures below and above the MS was conducted with or without prior ausforming (∼0.5 strain, 0.5 s−1 strain rate) in order to assess the influence of ausforming on subsequent transformation behaviour. The results suggest that when ausforming was applied above MS, it not only accelerated the bainite transformation kinetics, but also initiated strain-induced bainite/martensite formation. At temperatures below MS, prior ausforming did hinder the onset of bainite transformation, but the transformation rates were faster suggesting the strain-induced acceleration in kinetics. Due to a remarkable refinement of the bainitic structure achieved by prior ausforming in samples held below MS, the Vickers hardness improved appreciably unlike in the case of samples held above MS. Ausforming promoted significant refinement and uniformity of the bainitic plates, and also the orientations of the plates became more randomized. The dislocation density of RA decreased with the reduced content of secondary (fresh) martensite that formed during final cooling to room temperature.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Nanostructured bainite consisting of extremely fine plates (<50 nm) and thin retained austenite (RA) films has become well established in high carbon steels during the past two decades [ 1 , 2 ] and approaches for realization of such microstructures in medium-carbon (C) steels have also been attempted through specific composition and process designs [ 3 , 4 ]. The fineness of bainitic ferrite (BF) plates and RA films originates from low-temperature isothermal transformation and provides an excellent combination of ultra-high tensile strength (1700–2400 MPa), adequate ductility (up to 30%) and good fracture toughness (30–50 MPa m 1/2 ) [ 5 , 6 ].

Low-temperature isothermal transformation (<350 °C) is essential for achieving the extremely fine plates of bainitic ferrite, and in conventional approaches, steels with high C content (typically 0.7–1.1 wt% C) and consequent low martensite start (M S ) temperatures have been held at temperatures slightly above M S  for times ranging from a few hours to several weeks. However, in several studies during the past decades, efforts have been put to shorten the isothermal holding time for bainitic transformation above M S  as well as to lower the C content in order to improve the weldability and bendability without compromising on the mechanical properties [ 7–9 ]. Medium-C steels have exhibited nanostructured bainitic laths finer than 100 nm with corresponding Vickers hardness of the order of 600–650 HV, which was close to the typical hardness of the traditional high-C bainitic steels and higher than that of the conventional tempered martensite [ 3 , 10 ].

Low-temperature ausforming may refine the plate size as well as accelerate the kinetics of bainite transformation owing to an increase in the strength of austenite and ensuing dislocation density, though the benefits depend on the ausforming conditions. Thus, it should be emphasized that not all ausforming schedules provide these improvements and more attention should be paid on the process design leading to appropriate ausforming conditions [ 3 , 4 , 7–17 ]. For instance, Hu et al. [ 14 ] reported that ausforming of the medium-carbon steels at ≤ 400 °C accelerated the bainite formation, whereas ausforming at slightly elevated temperatures of 450 °C or 500 °C actually decelerated the transformation kinetics. However, properly designed low-temperature ausforming can be highly beneficial, especially for low-C and medium-C steels, where low transformation temperatures (<300 °C), required for the refinement of the bainitic ferrite to the nanostructured level, are unviable due to relatively higher M S  compared to those of steels with high C contents. The reduction of M S  via ausforming seems to be negligible [ 12 ], while recently strain-induced and stress-induced transformation from austenite into martensite and/or bainite have recently been shown to occur during ausforming above M S  but below 500 °C, especially in the temperature range 300–400 °C, which led to significantly higher flow stresses and eventually required high rolling forces [ 15–17 ].

So far as the role of ausforming on the RA is concerned, even a small amount of ausforming at 600 °C followed by isothermal holding above 350 °C increased the fraction of blocky-shaped RA, whereas only a nominal decrease in holding temperature by 25 °C improved the stability of RA remarkably, regardless of the amount of strain imparted during ausforming [ 12 ]. Besides, the blocky martensite/austenite (M/A) constituents that formed as a result of high-temperature bainitic holding, had a deteriorating effect on the room temperature (RT) toughness.

Another approach to refine the BF plates is to apply the isothermal transformation of austenite to bainite below the M S  in steels, which has been investigated using steels with various C contents [ 18–30 ]. In general, the outcome of the studies suggests that in low-C and medium-C steels, the transformation rate will increase when some martensite is introduced in the microstructure prior to holding for bainite formation, as the newly formed martensite/austenite interfaces provide more autocatalytic nucleation sites [ 26 , 29 , 30 ].

Besides, the combined effects of both ausforming as well as bainite transformation below M S  in low- and medium-C steels have recently been reported in the literature [ 31 , 32 ]. According to Zhao et al. [ 31 ], ausforming at temperatures 20–30 °C above M S  and subsequent austempering at temperatures below M S  not only refined the BF plates but decreased the size of brittle M/A blocks, which are known to be detrimental to toughness. Hu et al. [ 32 ] reported that strong misorientation gradients, which had developed due to ausforming below M S , actually delayed the onset of a transformation of austenite into bainite and later on, hindered the growth of bainite, since the misorientation gradients in effect faded the orientation relationship between austenite and new bainite.

The present study aims at understanding and clarifying the effects of ausforming on the evolving microstructural characteristics of nanostructured bainite in medium-C steel alloyed with Mn, Si, Mo, and Cr, especially when both the ausforming strain and subsequential isothermal holding were applied at the same temperature below M S  temperature comprising varying fractions of primary martensite (in the range 5–45 °C below M S ). In addition, similar ausforming and subsequent isothermal holding treatments were conducted at two temperatures slightly above M S  temperature (20 and 45 °C above M S  temperature) in order to be able to compare the microstructural features with those of the tests conducted below M S  temperature and elucidate the nature of bainite formation. A series of physical simulation experiments were accordingly planned on a Gleeble 3800® thermomechanical simulator to unravel the influence of primary martensite, dislocation density and conditions of bainite formation on the characteristics of evolving nanostructured bainite in the medium-C steel following ausforming and subsequent isothermal holding below M S  temperature and results compared with those obtained above M S  temperature.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs:
The chemical composition of the medium-C steel used in the present investigation is presented in  Table 1 
                      . Also included in the table are the corresponding bainite start (B S ) and M S  temperatures, as well as the melting point (T m ). A commercial thermodynamic-kinetic software IDS [ 33 ], which combines a microstructural tool developed to simulate the non-equilibrium solidification of steels, was used for the alloy design to minimize the chemical inhomogeneity due to interdendritic segregation during casting. Meanwhile, the steel should be able to impart adequate hardenability by alloying 2.0 wt% Mn and 1.0 wt% Cr, see  Table 1 . While M S  temperature was estimated by using Andrews’ equation modified by Kung and Rayment [ 34 ], B S  temperature was determined by JMatPro® v12.0 software in order to estimate appropriate isothermal holding times at various temperatures close to M S  temperature [ 35 ], and T m  was estimated using Thermo-Calc® version 2020b equipped with Scheil solidification model [ 36 ]. The steel was alloyed with a high level of Si (1.5%) in order to retard carbide precipitation and/or growth during the isothermal holding, yet the complete prevention of precipitation was infeasible [ 37–39 ]. Mo was added for enhanced strengthening effect via grain refinement at high temperatures and subsequent refinement of BF [ 6 ].

Since strain-induced phase transformation was expected to occur during the course of low-temperature ausforming treatment [ 17 , 40 ], additional experiments were conducted in order to understand and record the flow stress characteristics at temperatures (T def ) above B S  (T def  = 400 °C, 500 °C, and 600 °C) to be able to compare with those of samples undergoing ausforming and bainitizing in order to discern possible occurrence of stress and/or strain-induced transformation during isothermal holding (at 325, 300, 275, 255, 235 °C). In these experiments, the samples were reheated to 1100 °C, held for 2 min, cooled down to T def  followed by uniaxial compression to a true strain of 0.5 at 0.5 s −1 , and cooled down to RT without a subsequent isothermal holding.

Samples were then cut in half along the compression axis in order to perform the metallographic investigation in the centre of the samples. Vickers hardness was measured using an indentation load of 5 kg, and the results were reported as an average and standard error of at least five measurements for each specimen. The microstructures were studied using a Zeiss Sigma field-emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. FESEM observations were made on polished (1 μm diamond paste) and etched (Nital, 2% nitric acid) surfaces of the samples at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV at a working distance of 5 mm using an in-lens detector. Another polishing round with colloidal silica was conducted before the EBSD measurements in FESEM. During EBSD scanning, FESEM was operated using 15 kV accelerating voltage at a working distance of 15 mm. A step size of 0.05 μm was used and the scanned area for each map was approximately 45 × 45 μm. A JEOL 2200FS energy-filtered/scanning transmission electron microscope (TEM) was used for the detailed metallographic study. The focused ion beam (FIB) technique was employed to section thin lamellas from the specimens for subsequent TEM analysis. The TEM was operated at 200 kV enabling a good resolution at high magnifications to clarify the evolution and co-existence of different phases and precipitates. Accordingly, selected area electron diffraction (SAD) patterns were recorded and analysed to identify the corresponding phases and precipitates were studied. sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: Hereinafter, the ausformed samples are referred to as AF-T where “T” is the corresponding isothermal holding temperature. For instance, AF-325 refers to the sample ausformed and isothermally held at 325 °C. Similarly, non-ausformed samples are referred to as ND-T.

sections.heading: Flow stress behaviour
paragraphs:
The true stress – true strain curves corresponding to ausforming at all the five temperatures (from 235 to 325 °C) are shown in  Fig. 2 
                         a and corresponding temperature deviations (ΔT) from the nominal deformation temperatures are presented in  Fig. 2 b. Exceptionally high flow stress levels were observed at 235 °C and 255 °C, together with appreciable temperature rise during the deformation. For instance, during compression at 235 °C, the temperature rise was as high as 285 °C at a strain of 0.3 and up to 325 °C at a strain of 0.5. The temperature rise due to phase transformation and/or adiabatic heating based on mean flow stress was estimated in a way similar to the authors’ previous study [ 17 ], which suggested that under the given conditions, the latent heat release essentially due to phase transformation, might increase the temperature by approximately 120 °C at 235 °C and by 50 °C at 300 °C (measured 90 and 36 °C, respectively, in Gleeble; see  Fig. 2 b). However, the formula used in the calculation of temperature rise did not consider strain rate, as the effect can be small at the low strain rate of 0.5 s −1 . Nevertheless, the occurrence of strain-induced phase transformation could not be explicitly revealed. Besides, the rise in the temperature caused mainly by phase transformation could delay or prevent the strain-induced martensitic transformation. Further investigation on the presence of the strain-induced martensite was carried out using the JC model on the flow stress behaviour to exclude plausible aberrations/deviations in the flow stress caused by strain-induced phase transformation.

JC model fitting was conducted for engineering stress-strain data obtained at 600 °C in a relatively narrow strain range of 0.05–0.2, see the fitted (dotted line) and experimental (full line) curves in  Fig. 3 
                         a. The strain range was strictly restricted to low strains to ensure that fitting was done in the absence of any strain-induced phase transformation. The corresponding fitted material constants  A ,  B, n , and  m  are shown in  Table 3 
                         . Typical curves predicted with the JC model at lower temperatures, i.e. 300 °C (above M S ) and 235 °C (below M S ) together with experimental engineering stress-strain curves are shown in  Fig. 3 b and c, respectively. Corresponding strain hardening rates are plotted in  Fig. 3 e and f, respectively. In the case of 300 °C, the JC model deviated from the experimental flow stress after approximately 0.19 strain. The aberration resembled the flow behaviour related to strain-induced bainite formation at low-temperature ausforming reported in the authors’ earlier research [ 17 ]. Meanwhile, the strain hardening rate at 300 °C ( Fig. 3 e) remained almost constant or slightly increased after 0.1 strain, which should not occur without the presence of a strain-induced martensite or bainite [ 15 , 16 , 48 , 49 ]. On the other hand, a sharp increase of 36 °C in the temperature during the deformation at 300 °C (see  Fig. 3 b) could cause a decrease in the flow stress, but no such signs were observed. As expected, the engineering stress-strain curve of specimen deformed below M S  at 235 °C stayed well above the JC model predictions, as approximately 36% of austenite had already transformed into primary martensite during cooling to 235 °C (see  Table 3 ) and the parameters of JC model were actually based on the flow stress of austenite. Nevertheless, after 0.4 strain a slight increase in the strain hardening rate ( Fig. 3 f) implied the occurrence of phase transformation of the untransformed austenite to bainite, yet the temperature of the sample had already risen by approximately 90 °C until that point, see  Fig. 2 b. The same was observed in the case of sample ausformed at 255 °C as well, though a lesser extent. Hence, the occurrence of strain-induced phase transformation can already be discerned from the experimental flow stress behaviour.

sections.heading: Determination of M S  temperature and primary martensite fraction
paragraphs:
In order to choose appropriate isothermal holding temperatures for bainite formation, M S  temperature was first estimated with a modified Andrews’ equation and verified experimentally as an average of five measurements. Typical dilatation curves used for the evaluation of M S  are shown in  Fig. 4 
                            a. The plateau in the initial part of the transformation is due to the inhomogeneity of the microstructure [ 50 ], which is typical of casted and non-homogenized medium-C steels, especially with Mn and Cr alloying [ 51 , 52 ]. Cooling at the rate 50 °Cs −1  resulted in slightly higher M S  temperature compared to that at 10 °Cs −1  (285 °C vs. 275 °C), which is within the scatter band. However, no clear trend could be seen considering the entire data comprising cooling at different rates in the range 5–50 °Cs −1 . sections.heading: Bainite formation during the isothermal holding
paragraphs:
Relative changes in diameter recorded during the course of the isothermal holding at all five temperatures are shown in  Fig. 5 
                            a and b. The results suggest that the effect of prior ausforming on the subsequent phase transformation kinetics was significantly different for the specimens held isothermally above (300 and 325 °C) and below (235 and 255 °C) the M S , while the effect was small, when the deformation was applied just a few degrees below M S  (275 °C). In other words, the higher the fraction of primary martensite, the more was the hindering effect of deformation on the phase transformation kinetics. In good agreement with the results of Hu et al. [ 32 ], deformation at the lowest two temperatures below M S  (235, 255 °C) appreciably retarded the onset of the bainite transformation, thereby delaying the start from ∼30 s to 1000 s at 235 °C, and from 1 s to 80 s at 255 °C. It should be emphasized that the onset of the bainite formation at 235 °C was not seen in  Fig. 5 b, since the specimen contracted prior to bainite formation due to an occurrence of a competing phenomenon, presumably tempering of the primary martensite. Deformation just below M S  at 275 °C, however, did not significantly affect the onset time of bainite transformation. In contrast, above M S , the onset of bainite transformation in AF samples occurred almost 1–2 orders of magnitude quicker than in ND samples. Without prior ausforming, the onset of bainite transformation was fastest at the lowest two temperatures below M S , as a consequence of pre-existing martensite in the microstructure, as also reported by Zhao et al. [ 31 ]. At the highest three temperatures (325, 300, and 275 °C) ausforming resulted in relatively higher fractions of bainite formed compared to ND-specimens, while the difference was far more significant at 300 °C and 325 °C than at 275 °C, see  Fig. 5 .

sections.heading: Secondary martensite formation
paragraphs:
Dilatation measurements showing the relative change in diameters of ND and AF specimens plotted against temperature during the final cooling from isothermal holding temperature to RT is shown in  Fig. 6 
                            a and b, respectively. In most ND samples (except probably 255 °C) a fraction of carbon-enriched austenite transformed into martensite during the final cooling marked by significant inflexions in the dilatation curves. However, the AF samples did not exhibit such strong indication of phase transformation. Based on the K-M fitting shown in  Fig. 4 b, the estimated secondary martensite fractions were 17%, <2%, 5%, 10% and 10% for ND-235, ND-255, ND-275, ND-300 and ND-325, respectively. In comparison, the AF samples contained low fractions of secondary martensite (<2%), except for AF-325 sample, which had a marginally higher fraction of ∼3%. The plateaus at the initial stage of the final cooling were found in the dilatation curves of most samples and appeared quite extended over wide temperature ranges (30–70 °C depending on the isothermal holding temperature) for AF samples compared to ND samples. The plateaus mark the continuation of the bainite formation during final cooling, which can be accelerated as the temperature drops at the start of the final cooling. While the nucleation of bainitic ferrite at temperatures concerned may take typically more than 1000 s at 235 °C (see  Fig. 5 b), the growth of already existing plates may proceed without delay at a rate just sufficient to balance the thermal contraction during the cooling. Also, the effect of chemical inhomogeneity on the phase transformation temperatures should not be disregarded in the discussion, but this is out of the scope of the present study [ 50 , 56 ].

sections.heading: Phase fractions estimated from the dilatation behaviour
paragraphs:
Based on the summary of the dilatation results elucidated in sections  3.2.1 to 3 .2.3 and the corresponding results obtained from XRD analysis (see chapter 3.5), the phase fractions could be roughly estimated, as shown in  Table 5 
                            . In the case of AF samples, the fractions of strain-induced martensite remained unclear, but the same were estimated after determining the fractions of other phases and considered as f SIM .

sections.heading: FESEM micrographs and (macro) hardness
paragraphs:
FESEM images recorded on the ND and AF specimens held above M S  are shown in  Fig. 7 
                            a, c, and  Fig. 7 b, d, respectively. Corresponding Vickers hardness (± standard error) and RA fractions are also shown on the micrographs for ready comparison. Similarly, the microstructures recorded on ND and AF samples held below M S  are presented in  Fig. 8 
                            a, c, e and  Fig. 8 b, d, f, respectively, along with their Vickers hardness and RA fractions shown on the micrographs. The compression axis is almost vertical in the case of FESEM images of AF samples. The RA fractions shown in  Fig. 7 a–d and  Fig. 8 a–f are rounded to the closest integers, and more detailed information is given in  Table 6 
                            . The annotations in  Figs. 7 and 8  are primary martensite (PM), secondary martensite (SM), bainitic ferrite (BF), and retained austenite (RA). It is noticeable that the M/A constituents have not been annotated in the figures, since practically all the SM was formed in typical islands, except ND-235, in which SM appeared everywhere in the microstructure without the existence of the typical islands.
Above M S :

The microstructure of the ND-325 sample ( Fig. 7 a) consisted of BF, RA, and SM, see  Table 5  for fractions. Morphology of BF varied from thin (20–100 nm) and long (>5 μm) plates to more irregular plates, which were thicker (>500 nm) and occasionally shorter (<2 μm). The FESEM images also displayed thin BF plates organized in long, straight sheaves, stretching as long as 40–50 μm, even across the prior austenite grains. Thin plates in such sheaves were surrounded by curved, white features with the typical morphology very similar, but bigger than cementite carbides, measuring a mean width of approximately between 20 and 50 nm. As will be presented later, TEM study identified these curly features as thin austenite films, sometimes called interwoven austenite [ 57 ]. In addition, RA films (50–200 nm) also existed between the irregular BF plates as well as in coarse M/A islands of sizes about 3–8 μm long and from 1 to 2 μm wide M/A islands. SM could be distinguished in M/A islands because of its typical etching contrast, whereas RA was non-etched and remained featureless, as also reported elsewhere [ 12 , 24 ]. RA is often found at the edges of M/A constituents, since excess carbon partitioned from BF to untransformed austenite moves to the BF/RA interfaces before diffusing in austenite, which is much slower austenite than in the BF. Hence, the areas far away from the boundaries of the austenite may not receive enough carbon needed for stabilization at RT and thus, transform to SM during final cooling. Similar morphologies of BF, martensite and RA in medium-C steel after isothermal holding above M S  have been reported by Navarro-Lopez et al. [ 24 ].

In comparison, BF observed in AF-325 sample comprised similar thin (20–100) nm plates across the prior austenite grains, but the sheaves of bainite were shorter in length and more randomized than in ND-325. Based on the dilatation analysis (see 3.2.3), the fraction of SM was estimated to be about 3%, yet it was difficult to discern in the FESEM micrographs. Flow stress behaviour and related temperature rise during ausforming (see  Fig. 2 ) suggested the occurrence of the strain-induced phase transformation. However, it was not clear whether the strain-induced phase was martensite or bainite. The sheaves growing from different prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs) intersected with each other forming a criss-cross pattern, as also reported in ausformed steels by many authors [ 7 , 58 ]. The criss-cross pattern formed in AF-325 made the bainitic structure look relatively more complex and randomized, and hence, it could be assumed that empty space for large M/A islands was not remaining after isothermal holding as in the case of ND-325. Similar effects of ausforming have been reported by Zhao et al. [ 31 ]. Moreover, the increased strength and hence dislocation density of austenite due to the ausforming resisted the growth of the sheaves and refined the average plate thickness. Although the ausforming significantly refined the average plate thickness and irregular/granular shaped bainite plates were absent in AF-325, some coalesced plates (>200 nm) still existed, especially in the vicinity of the intersections either of bainite sheaves or PAGBs. Unlike ND-325, the curly, and thin RA was not present in AF-325 and most RA appeared as relatively coarse 50–200 nm films. Though M/A islands were not present in AF-325, still blocky, rectangular or triangular RA constituents about 0.5–1.0 μm wide, could be observed.

ND-300 ( Fig. 7 c) showed similar characteristics of BF, SM, and RA as seen in ND-325 ( Fig. 7 a), though some differences can be pointed out. The morphology of BF was mostly thin (20–100 nm) and long (>5 μm) plates, but the sheaves were shorter, and the plates were not as well organized as observed in the case of ND-325 ( Fig. 7 a). Irregular plates and granular-type bainite existed frequently, though the width (200–400 nm) of the plates was not as coarse as seen in ND-325 (>500 nm). Curved, thin white RA films were also observed adjacent to the thin BF plates, and RA was also seen in M/A islands, though not as large as in ND-325 (>500 nm). M/A islands were from 0.5 to 2 μm wide and from 2 to 4 μm long, typically rectangular or triangular located either alongside the PAGB or at the intersection of multiple BF sheaves. Rarely could be M/A islands seen in such areas where parallel sheaves travelled all the way from PAGB to another PAGB. The difference in f RA  between ND-325 (17%) and ND-300 (13%) can be explained in terms of lack of large M/A islands in ND-300, while the higher hardness in ND-300 (548 HV5 vs. 505 HV5) originated mainly from finer thin BF plates as well as overall refinement of BF plates (86 nm vs. 124 nm), besides lower f RA . Although ND-300 and AF-325 had similar average t BF , the hardness of ND-300 was ∼40 HV higher than that of AF-325, obviously due to the presence of twice f RA  in AF-325. Similarly as AF-325, AF-300 ( Fig. 7 d) resembled lot the BF typically seen in ausformed steels [ 7 ], without any signs of large M/A islands or fine, high-carbon SM. Hence, the differences between the microstructural features of AF-300 and AF-325 were insignificant, although the AF-300 had slightly lower f RA , and more refined average t BF , besides a higher dislocation density.
Below M S :

BF observed in ND-275 ( Fig. 8 a) generally consisted of thick (100–500 nm) and somewhat long (2–5 μm) coalesced plates without carbides, besides the presence of a few thin (40–100 nm) plates existed as well. The sheaves were not as parallel as observed in bainite obtained above M S  ( Fig. 7 a and c), presumably due to various new nucleation sites on martensite-austenite interfaces due to the presence of PM [ 24 , 59 ]. Therefore, as BF could nucleate at multiple locations other than PAGBs, the identification of PAGBs in FESEM images was not as obvious as in the samples held above M S . The presence of tempered PM appearing as featureless dark regions with typical morphology of long (5–10 μm) and wide (200–500 nm) acicular plates also made the difference from samples held above M S  and are often difficult to distinguish from thick BF plates. As will be presented later, curved interwoven austenite films were observed via TEM investigations, similarly as in the case of ND-325 and ND-300. Although large RA blocks were not present in the microstructure, small M/A constituents (0.2–0.5 μm wide, 1.0–2.0 μm long) comprising SM and RA could still be detected.

In comparison, M/A islands of the same size and morphology as seen in ND-275 were also detected in AF-275, though only locally in certain regions, presumably because of the chemical inhomogeneity in the sample. In AF-275, RA existed as thin films (even as fine as 20 nm) surrounded by thin BF plates (20–100 nm), besides the presence of small RA blocks (300–500 nm wide) within the intersections of the BF sheaves (criss-cross pattern), and few thick films (100–200 nm) in the vicinity of thick PM plates (200–600 μm). The significant difference between AF-275 from ND-275 was the presence of PM ( Fig. 8 c), which looked slightly curvilinear and very similar to wedge-like bainite sheaves, along with finely divided thin films and blocks of RA (10–20 nm).

Nevertheless, BF in ND-255 occurred mostly as thin (30–100 nm), long (>2 μm) plates with finely divided RA films of similar thickness,  Fig. 8 c. Interestingly though, the characteristics of BF and t BF  size distribution appeared close to ND-300 instead of ND-275. Small RA blocks of ∼0.5 μm width and 1–2 μm length were also present in the microstructure. The difference from ND-275 was pronounced in terms of RA, as the latter contained long RA films (2–8 μm) which were not only divided in PM, but also in parallel BF plates.

BF plate thickness distributions in ND and AF samples are presented in  Fig. 9 
                            a and b, respectively. The values in parentheses represent the average t BF  of at least 100 plates for each sample with standard error. Due to the insufficient number of recognizable bainite plates, both ND-235 and AF-235 were not considered in this study. The comparison. Ausforming not only refined the t BF , but also rendered the distribution close to the average value suggesting higher peaks and more uniformity of the BF in the microstructure. In the case samples isothermally held at 300 °C, the influence of ausforming on the plate thickness was the least obvious, as the difference from ND samples in respect of t BF  was very small (86 ± 4 nm and 74 ± 4 nm for ND-300 and AF-300, respectively). In ND-300, 66% of the plates were fine (≤100 nm), whereas in AF-300, this fraction was slightly higher at 76%. Interestingly though, the hardness of ND-300 (548 HV) was the same as that of AF-300 (550 HV), obviously because a significantly higher fraction of RA in AF-300 (20%) compared to that of ND-300 (12%). The most significant influence of ausforming on subsequent BF refinement was obtained at 255 °C, as the average t BF  of ND-255 (88 ± 4 nm) was more than four times the average of the AF-255 (21 ± 1 nm), see  Fig. 9 . Besides, nearly all the plates were fine in AF-255, while about two-thirds of the plates in ND-255 were fine (≤100 nm). The greatest absolute influence of ausforming was observed at 275 °C, where the t BF  improved to 57 ± 3 nm in AF-275 compared to 139 ± 9 nm obtained in ND-275. Moreover, the fraction of fine BF (≤100 nm) was only about 30% in ND-275, compared to 80% fine plates seen in AF-275.

sections.heading: EBSD analysis
paragraphs:
In order to detect and understand the distribution of phases and crystallographic orientation relationships between different phase constituents, i.e. bainitic ferrite (BF), secondary martensite (SM), strain-induced martensite (SIM), tempered martensite (TM) and retained austenite (RA), EBSD measurements of all ND and AF samples were performed.  Fig. 10 
                             a, d and  Fig. 11 
                             a, d present the inverse pole figure (IPF) maps of ND and AF specimens, isothermally held at 325 °C and 300 °C, respectively. Different colours signify the different crystallographic orientations of phase constituents. A significant difference in crystallographic orientation was noticed for BF between ND and AF specimens. Whereas a strong orientation towards certain crystallographic planes was observed in ND specimens, multiple crystallographic orientations existed within the BF sheaves in AF specimens. Guo et al. [ 9 ] studied the effect of ausforming strain on low-temperature bainitic transformation kinetics of a high-C, high-Si/Al steel. A similar orientation relationship was observed for ausformed specimens with random alignment in different crystallographic directions compared to a strong texture seen in ND sample. It is widely recognized that during deformation, the dislocation structure formed on the active slip plane possibly acts as the preferential nucleation site of BF, and the active slip plane would then become the habit plane of BF plates, which makes the growth direction of BF plate almost parallel to this plane [ 7 ]. However, the ausforming process can drastically reduce the number of variants in a single austenite grain. With decreasing ausforming temperature, the variant selection tendency becomes more obvious ( Fig. 11 d). The combined image quality (IQ) and phase maps of ND and AF specimens are presented in  Fig. 10 b,e and  Fig. 11 b,e respectively. The green colour corresponds to the finely divided RA blocks/films, whereas the red colour corresponds to all BCC transformation products (bainite/martensite). The darker regions in the combined IQ + phase maps ( Fig. 10 b,e and  Fig. 11 b,e) indicate lower IQ level, which corresponds to the grains or regions with a higher density of lattice imperfections, such as dislocations and point defects, essentially associated with SM and SIM. The combined IQ + phase maps as presented in  Fig. 10 b,e indicate that high-C martensite islands exist among the bainite, while the presence of local wavy-shaped, band-like darker regions along and/or within the prior austenite grain boundaries in  Fig. 11 b and e correspond to SIM, thus corroborating the dilatation results, see  Table 5 . Besides the strips of film-like RA, blocky morphology was also discernible, located between BF plates and martensitic laths and dispersed randomly in both ND-325 and ND-300 samples ( Fig. 10 b,d). Ausforming significantly reduced the size of film-like RA and increased its fraction and wider distribution ( Fig. 11 b,e), thus corroborating the XRD results.

In order to quantify the local grain misorientation due to lattice distortion, Kernel average misorientations (KAM) of ND-325 and ND-300 specimens were measured and the corresponding maps are presented in  Fig. 10 c and f and  Fig. 11 c and f, respectively. The KAM value reflects the transformation strain accommodated by geometrically necessary dislocations. In ND-325 and 300 specimens, the KAM values in the vicinity of RA/BF interfaces were found to be slightly higher. Furthermore, KAM in SM was expectedly higher than in RA or BF. Significant dislocation density due to phase transformation was observed in the BF matrix, whereas the interface regions in AF specimens consisted of slightly higher dislocation densities, indicating the existence of low-angle grain boundaries. The KAM maps of AF-325 and AF-300 specimens exhibited a significant variation in the local misorientation within highly distorted bainite plate boundaries. This signified the local variation of dislocation density in the matrix. The high level of KAM value corresponding to the wavy band-like regions further confirmed the presence of SIM structure.

IPF maps of the ND specimens isothermally held at different temperatures below M S  are presented in  Fig. 12 
                            a,d,g, respectively. Similarly as seen in the case of ND specimens tested above M S  ( Fig. 10 a,d), these specimens ( Fig. 12 a,d,g) also revealed that BF plates were mostly aligned with specific crystallographic directions. Following ausforming below M S , a random orientation was noticed, and the variant selection tendency seemed to reduce with a decrease in the ausforming temperature ( Fig. 13 
                            a,d,g). The number of bainitic ferrite variants in a single austenite grain was drastically reduced by ausforming. A very strong variant selection was observed in AF-235 specimen, related to the operation of active slip systems operating in austenite during the deformation, which became the preferential nucleation sites during bainite transformation.

The combined IQ and phase maps of corresponding ND and AF specimens tested below Ms, are presented in  Fig. 12 b,e, h and  Fig. 13 b,e,h respectively. The presence of SM was noticed in ND-275, ND-255 and ND-235 specimens ( Fig. 12 b,e,h) and the corresponding fraction increased with the decrease in isothermal holding temperature. On the other hand, ausforming at lower temperatures gradually accelerated the formation of SIM as observed from  Fig. 13 b,e and h. Apart from SM/SIM, relatively thicker PM lath structures were also discernible in all ND and AF specimens, as marked in  Fig. 12 b,e,h and  Fig. 13 b,e,h, respectively. Overall, these observations corroborated well with the dilatation results ( Table 6 ). A clear reduction of RA fractions with decreasing isothermal holding temperature, both in ND and AF conditions, agreed well with the XRD results, though very fine films of RA (<80 nm) cannot be revealed due to the resolution limit of the EBSD facility.

The KAM maps of ND and AF specimens isothermally held at different temperatures below M S  are presented in  Fig. 12 c,f,I and  Fig. 13 c,f,i respectively. The maps revealed that high local misorientations were mainly concentrated in the vicinity of SM and SIM phase constituents of ND and AF specimens, respectively. A high concentration of local misorientations indicated a more distorted internal structure. Relatively low KAM in some of the thicker martensite plates was present in both ND and AF specimens signifying them as PM, as significant recovery of dislocations is expected to take place during the isothermal holding.  Fig. 14 
                            a and b further compile the average quantified KAM values of ND and AF specimens, respectively. The average KAM value in the case of AF samples was found to increase with decreasing ausforming temperature. These results are in good agreement with the hardness of corresponding samples. However, no such clear trend was observed in ND specimens.
Acicular-shaped thick PM (200–600 μm) plates with high image quality and low KAM ( Fig. 13 b and c) clearly represented PM, which was probably the most significant difference from AF-325 and AF-300.

Equivalent circle diameter (ECD) distribution is often reported as a measure of the grain size including the phase constituents and related phase boundaries in the microstructure with misorientations >3°. At the same time, the typical morphology of bainite and martensite in the 2D observations is relatively thin but long laths and plates (see section  3.3.1 ). For the calculation of ECD, each plate or lath was considered equivalent to a circle with an area equal to that of the current plate or lath and then the equivalent diameter of the circle was determined. Though ECD measurements are not practical with bainitic and martensitic microstructures, such measurements made on  ND  and  AF  samples, as presented in  Fig. 17 
                            a and b, respectively, were found to support the estimated t BF  measured in FESEM images of this study (see  Fig. 9 ), thus clarifying the overall refinement of bainite and martensite achieved due to ausforming in the studied samples.

sections.heading: TEM characterization
paragraphs:
Due to the limited spatial resolution of the EBSD technique, the samples were further examined in TEM to characterize the detailed features of BF and RA down to the nanometre level, as well as to confirm the orientation relationship between RA and BF. The typical TEM bright field micrograph of ND-300 sample is shown in  Fig. 18 
                            a. In contrast to the classical structure of bainite as an aggregate of BF laths containing interlath or intralath carbides, the microstructure of bainite consisted of BF plates together with thin curved interwoven films of RA.  Fig. 18 b presents the magnified image of the region marked with a square in  Fig. 18 a. The presence of both curved, interwoven RA located inside the BF plate, and fine lamellar RA films located at BF plate boundaries, was confirmed as seen in  Fig. 18 a. Apart from the curved and thin film-like RA, blocky RA was also noticed in a few locations, as shown in  Fig. 18 b. The selected area diffraction (SAD) pattern of RA recorded on the [−112]γ zone axis and the corresponding TEM dark field image taken from the selected (220) spot are shown in  Fig. 18 c, which illustrates the presence of different types of RA. The presence of twinned martensite (SM) was also located in  Fig. 18 b and it appeared embedded inside the blocky M/A constituents, as revealed in the dark field image ( Fig. 18 c). This indicates that the SM transformation from austenite occurred during final cooling to RT following isothermal holding at 300 °C, presumably due to insufficient carbon enrichment within blocky RA.

Ausforming at 300 °C refined the size of BF plates and affected their morphology. Relatively thinner BF plates (needle-like) were observed in the AF-300 sample compared to ND-300, and the representative TEM bright field micrograph is shown in  Fig. 18 d. Such an observation was quite consistent with the observations made by FESEM microscopy ( Fig. 9 a and b). The high dislocation density in the BF plates was clearly revealed in the bright field image ( Fig. 18 d and e). The SAD pattern of RA was recorded on the [011]γ zone axis ( Fig. 18 f) and the corresponding dark field image taken from the selected (200) spot is presented in  Fig. 18 f. A large number of defects introduced through the ausforming process provided additional nucleation sites for BF plates to form and grow leading to an extensive refinement of BF because of the impingement effect [ 61 ]. However, the defects caused by ausforming possibly resisted the growth of bainite, which led to sluggish or incomplete bainitic transformation [ 31 , 62 ]. The existence of mainly fine film-like RA was seen in AF-300 ( Fig. 18 e and f) together with fine blocky RA. The size of blocky RA was markedly reduced as a result of prior ausforming, in comparison to that seen in the ND condition  Fig. 18 b and c.

TEM examination of ND-275 ( Fig. 19 
                            a,b,c) revealed similar RA morphology (curved and thin films) as noticed in the ND-300 ( Fig. 18 a,b,c). Isothermal holding at 275 °C did not introduce any appreciable change in the microstructure compared to ND-300, but resulted in a reduction of the size of blocky RA,  Fig. 19 b and c. Furthermore, the average film thickness of RA was slightly refined although the t BF  was quite similar to ND-300 sample. A clear reduction of the BF plate length after ausforming treatment at 275 °C was distinguishable, as seen in the bright field image of AF-275,  Fig. 19 d,e,f. The SAD pattern of RA recorded on the [110]γ zone axis was indexed to identify diffraction spots for RA and the corresponding dark field image taken on the selected (200) spot is presented in  Fig. 19 e and f, respectively. The existence of mainly fine film-like RA together with fine blocky RA was seen to be present in the microstructure,  Fig. 19 f.

The presence of twinned martensite was noticed below M S  in ND-255, as shown in  Fig. 20 
                            a. The SAD pattern of RA was recorded on the [011]γ zone axis is presented in  Fig. 20 b. The corresponding dark field image recorded on the selected (200) spot is presented in  Fig. 20 c. Only film-like RA was noticed in  Fig. 20 f. A significant refinement of BF plate in respect of thickness as well as length was obtained by prior ausforming treatment at 255 °C. The maximum true thickness of the BF was lower than 100 nm, which was in the scale of the nanostructured bainite. The SAD pattern of RA recorded on the [111]γ zone axis and the corresponding dark field image taken on the selected (110) spot is presented in  Fig. 20 e, showing only film-like RA. Moreover, some accommodation twins were observed in the RA caused due to the plastic deformation introduced by the bainitic transformation [ 63 ]. The microstructures obtained in samples isothermally held below M S  became refined due to three possible reasons: (i) Increased strength of austenite adjacent to newly formed primary martensite, (ii) increased dislocation density and (iii) Increase in the driving force due to the decrease in isothermal holding temperature and thus, enhanced nucleation rate for bainitic transformation [ 4 , 41 , 61 , 64 ].

The presence of primary martensite lath was observed along with nanoscale BF ( Fig. 20 d). A higher magnification micrograph of the framed region in (d) is shown in  Fig. 20 g, which clearly depicted the characteristics of primary martensitic lath structure. Generally, the change in shape due to martensite transformation accompanies internal stresses. The presence of dislocation tangles within PM was clearly seen in the magnified image of the framed region in (g), as shown in  Fig. 20 h. The existence of dislocation tangles in martensitic laths indicates that a low temperature (255 °C) partial tempering treatment is insufficient to fully annihilate high-density dislocations. The presence of a small fraction of carbides on tangled dislocations of PM ( Fig. 20 i) suggests that a strong driving force for carbides to precipitate even at the low isothermal holding temperature of 255 °C, despite the presence of 1.5 wt% Si in the steel. These needle-like carbides of ∼15 nm width have a hexagonal crystal structure. The interplanar spacing measured from SAD pattern on [121]η zone axis confirmed the presence of η-carbides (Fe 2 C). The orientation relationship between the martensite (α) matrix and η-carbide is determined as (113)α//(121)η. The precipitation of Fe 2 C transition carbides was attributed to the slow diffusion rate of carbon in austenite during the low-temperature isothermal holding. Alloying with Si can delay carbide precipitation, but cannot completely prevent it because of the high driving force due to carbon enrichment locally, as also seen in authors’ previous work [ 27 , 37–39 ].

sections.heading: The evaluation of dislocation density in austenite based on XRD measurements
paragraphs:
The XRD patterns representing relative intensities of ND and AF samples are shown in  Fig. 21 
                         . Only the phases with body-centred cubic (BCC), body-centred tetragonal (BCT), and face-centred cubic (FCC) structures were considered for the analysis. As the samples consisted of multiple phases, the fitting of the experimental data with the Rietveld method was initially conducted twice for all the samples with two different presumptions: first with the consideration of BCC and FCC phases and secondly, considering BCT and FCC phases. After carefully checking the results and the goodness of the fitting, all further analyses were done using BCT and FCC as the present phases only. Dislocation densities introduced in both ND and AF samples were further evaluated from XRD data based on the principles of Williamson-Hall (W–H) line profile analysis and the obtained results are summarized in  Table 3 . The highest dislocation density for austenite was obtained in AF-235 (6.14 × 10 15  m −2 ), showing good agreement with the values reported by other researchers [ 25 , 30 ]. The dislocation density was seen to decrease linearly from 6.14 to 3.13 × 10 15  m −2  with increasing the ausforming temperature from 235 to 325 °C. It would be expected that the deformation prior to isothermal holding increases the BF nucleation rate, leading to limited growth of bainitic plates due to the strengthening of austenite through the introduction of dislocations by the ausforming [ 64 ]. Besides, dislocations enable mechanical stabilization of austenite and hence, retardation of the decomposition of austenite.

sections.heading: Factors affecting the overall hardness
paragraphs:
The f RA , C RA , dislocation density of austenite, and Vickers hardness of all ND and AF specimens are presented in ( Table 6 ). Vickers hardness, C RA , and dislocation density of RA as a function of f RA  are presented in  Fig. 22 
                          a, b, and c, respectively.

To understand the stability of RA, C RA  as a function of f RA  is shown in  Fig. 22 b. The general behaviour observed in the samples was unexpected: the greater the f RA  realized, the higher became the C RA  content. It is normally expected that the C RA  content would decrease, and approach towards the nominal carbon content (0.4%) with the increase in f RA . Nevertheless, the samples appeared to form three different groups in  Fig. 22 b: 1) ND samples above M S , 2) AF samples above M S , and 3) both ND and AF samples below M S . The first group of two points (ND-325 and ND-300) had mediocre f RA  but high C RA , while the second group (AF-325 and AF-300) possessed the highest two f RA,  despite having C RA  of the practically same level as the first group. The third group (all below M S  samples) consisted of samples which formed a trend of increasing C RA  with increasing f RA  at the lower end of f RA  values. Interestingly, the same trend was continued by the second group (AF-300 and AF-325) at high f RA  contents. The samples in the second and the third group which formed the general f RA -C RA  trend had one feature in common, strained austenite matrix, which was caused by either primary martensite (below M S ) or by ausforming (above M S ) or by the combination of both primary martensite and ausforming (AF-235, AF-255, AF-275). However, the first group in which the correlation between f RA  and C RA  followed the general slope but at relatively high C RA . Therefore, ausforming at above M S  temperatures stabilized higher fraction RA without compromising the stability of RA, as indicated by the similar C RA  level of ND and AF samples held above M S .

As regards the dislocation density of RA, the highest values were observed in samples with primary martensite (see  Fig. 22 c). Except for two samples, ND-275 and ND-300, the dislocation density dropped with increasing f RA  (see  Fig. 22 c). In other words, the higher the dislocation density of RA, the higher the fraction of phases formed at low temperatures (bainite, martensite). Therefore, the results could support the assumption that the higher dislocation density could introduce more nucleation sites for bainite and martensite and thus, accelerate the initiation of the phase transformation [ 26 , 29 , 30 ]. Avishan et al. reported a similar increase in dislocation density of RA when pre-existing martensite was introduced and retardation of carbon partitioning from BF into austenite due to high dislocation density on BF/austenite interfaces, but surprisingly, they also obtained more carbon enrichment in RA as a consequence of pre-existing martensite [ 30 ]. In this study, however, the pre-existing martensite had the quite opposite effect on the C RA , as the samples with pre-existing martensite had lower C RA  than other samples (see  Fig. 22 b). Da Silva et al. [ 59 ] reported practically identical f RA  (from 10 to 13%) regardless of whether the isothermal holding temperature was above or below M S , while the results deviated around the average without an obvious correlation between the isothermal temperatures and the f RA . In ND samples, the dislocation densities in austenite seem not to follow any trend with isothermal holding temperature (see  Fig. 22 c and  Table 6 ). This could be due to the different plate thickness of BF and different phase constituents (SM, PM, SIM etc.) obtained after isothermal holding at different temperatures. The formation of SIM/PM/SM induced deformation of the surrounding RA and thereby increased the dislocation density in the austenite.

sections.heading: Summary and conclusions
paragraphs:
Using physical simulation experiments in a Gleeble simulator, the combined effects of primary martensite along with prior ausforming, and resulting dislocation density in RA, were evaluated in respect of the formation of ultrafine/nanostructured bainite in medium-C steels at three isothermal holding temperatures below M S  temperature, and the results were compared with those obtained at two temperatures slightly above M S  temperature. The following conclusions can be drawn from this study. 
                         
                            • 
                            Low temperature ausforming to a true strain of 0.5 resulted in a significant rise in temperature (about 30–90 °C), increasing with the decrease in deformation temperature. The temperature rise was essentially due to strain induced martensite transformation, as the adiabatic rise in temperature cannot be significant because of low strain rate (0.5 s −1 ). 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Flow stress at low temperatures (≤325 °C) was predicted accurately using the JC model using the parameters obtained at 600 °C for the flow stress of austenite. The results suggest that at temperatures in the range 255–325 °C, strain-induced phase transformation caused deviations in the flow stress behaviour starting at about 0.2 strain. The flow stress curve at 235 °C did reveal such behaviour only after 0.4 strain, presumably due to the pre-existing large fraction of primary martensite (36%) and delay in the onset of bainite formation. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Prior ausforming accelerated the onset of bainite transformation at isothermal holding temperatures above M S , whereas at temperatures below M S , the onset of bainite formation was retarded. However, ausforming very close to M S  (∼5 °C below M S ) did not affect the onset time, nor the fraction of bainite formed. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            SM formation during the final cooling from isothermal holding temperature to RT was not suppressed by the presence of primary martensite in the microstructure. Instead, ausforming caused a reduction in SM fractions at all temperatures, due to the realization of significant strain-induced martensite/bainite, as well as high fractions of bainite formed during subsequent isothermal holding. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Ausforming refined the t BF , increased the f RA , and impeded subsequent SM transformation during the final cooling. Moreover, the orientations of BF plates were appreciably randomized, and the uniformity of BF plates increased as well. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The greatest refinement of BF as a result of ausforming was achieved at the isothermal holding temperature of 255 °C, as the average t BF  was reduced from 88 nm to 21 nm and all the plates were in the range of 10–90 nm. The refinement of BF was also reflected in respect of high Vickers hardness values of 507 HV5 and 619 HV5 realized in samples without or with prior ausforming, respectively. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Interestingly, at bainitizing temperatures above M S  (300, 325 °C), the changes in the microstructural features due to prior ausforming did not affect the overall Vickers hardness of the samples, indicating that a low-temperature ausformed steel could possess reasonably good ductility comparable to its non-deformed counterpart, without compromising on the gained high level of ultimate tensile strength. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            In non-deformed samples, the dislocation density of RA and Vickers hardness did not follow any general trend as a function of isothermal holding temperature, but dislocation density of RA decreased with ausforming, except at 300 °C. This indicates that the austenite, which accommodated relatively higher strains during ausforming as a result of strain partitioning, developed a higher dislocation density and transformed either to martensite/bainite due to strain induced transformation, or to ultrafine/nanostructured bainite during subsequent isothermal holding. Dislocations in the RA of non-deformed samples, however, originated mainly from the SM transformed during the final cooling and hence, the RA which accommodated the resulting strain caused by SM retained a high dislocation density.
